newsitem.title: CHINA: HK & Shanghai Hotels sees slower 2nd half.
newsitem.headline: HK & Shanghai Hotels sees slower 2nd half.

text.p: Hongkong and Shanghai Hotels Ltd will see a slowdown in earnings growth in second half 1997 due to weak demand in the remaining summer months and renovation work at the Kowloon Hotel, senior executives said on Thursday.
Hotel occupancy rates in the territory and in the company's hotels are also below expectations and could ease further, they said.

"The (hotel) industry in Hong Kong has been affected by the decrease in Japanese visitors in the first six months of 1997," said chief executive Pierre Boppe. "The biggest spending visitors (to Hong Kong) are the Japanese."

Last year was a strong year for the hotel industry worldwide, and it was an extremely good year for Hong Kong because of the strong promotion of Hong Kong as a destination by the Japanese tourist industry, Boppe said.
Japanese visitors to Hong Kong in 1997 are expected to fall to the 1995 level of 1.7 million visitors, compared with the 2.4 million in 1996, he added.

The company reported profit after tax and minority interests of HK$412 million for the six months ended June 30, up eight percent from HK$380 million in first half 1996, on the back of a 13 percent increase in turnover to HK$1.43 billion.

But profit attributable to shareholders fell five percent to HK$412 million from last year's HK$435 million, which included a windfall gain of HK$55 million from the sale of the company's 25 percent holding in Cathay Pacific Catering Services Ltd.
The results were slightly below expectations.
Operating profit rose five percent to HK$550 million, of which the hotel division accounted for HK$311 million, an increase of four percent over the year earlier period.
Rental income from investment properties rose to HK$233 million, an increase of eight percent.
The company's two principal revenue earners are its Hong Kong hotels, the Peninsula Hotel and the Kowloon Hotel.
"The occupancy rate at the Peninsula Hotel was just slightly higher than 1996, by one point, to 70 percent," said Boppe. "The average room rate rose about 10 percent to HK$3,500."

The Kowloon Hotel, on the other hand, saw a slight decline in its occupancy rate during the first half to around 85 percent, Boppe said, adding the average room rate rose about 10 percent to HK$1,000 per night.
Demand continues to be weaker than the company had forecast, Boppe said.
"Occupancy rates since June 1 are lower than 1996 and lower than our forecast, about 10 to 15 percent lower," he said. "But these are the worst two months of the year even in a strong year."

The company expanded its investment property portfolio during the year with the acquisition of the Quail Lodge of Carmel, California, in February and the formal opening of the Peak Tower in Hong Kong in May, a company statement said.

As for the company's controversial luxury hotel in Sydney, to be built near the Sydney Opera House, the company expected "before the end of August to receive a clear indication if we can proceed, " Boppe said.
The company hopes to complete a 229-room hotel by the year 2000 in time for the Sydney Olympics.
The company expects to complete The Peninsula Bangkok in 1998 and the The Peninsula Jakarta in 2000, the company said.
It was too early to say whether the depreciation of the Thai baht would have an adverse impact on the company, said Douglas Webster, director in charge of finance and corporate services.
"There is an effect of course (on operations), but it wouldn't be the same size as the percentage fall you are reading about," said Webster.
But as regards impact on the valuation of the Thai property, the company would wait until the end of the year before taking it into account, Webster said.
